source_refs.note: Book p. 94: 6.3 Arithmetic Mean definition, A = (a + b)/2, side Note on n A.M.s, Example 6. Teaching notes, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: A number \(A\) is said to be the A.M. (arithmetic mean) between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) if \(a, A, b\) are in A.P. If \(d\) is the common difference of this A.P., then \(A - a = d\) and \(b - A = d\). Thus

blocks.text_alt: A equals a plus b, over 2

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: If \(A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}, \ldots, A_{n}\) are said to be \(n\) A.M.s between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\), then \(a, A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}, \ldots, A_{n}, b\) are in A.P.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The A.M. is simply the average of the two numbers: add them and divide by 2. For example, the A.M. between 4 and 10 is \(\frac{4 + 10}{2} = 7\), and \(4, 7, 10\) is an A.P. with \(d = 3\).
On the number line the A.M. lies exactly half-way between \(a\) and \(b\).
Inserting \(n\) A.M.s between \(a\) and \(b\) means filling the gap with \(n\) numbers so that the whole list is an A.P. The list then has \(n + 2\) terms: \(a\) is the first term and \(b\) is the \((n + 2)\)th term. So \(d\) comes from \(b = a + (n + 1)d\).

blocks.title: Example 6
steps:
Given: \(a = \sqrt{2}\), \(b = 3\sqrt{2}\), three A.M.s to insert.
To find: \(A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}\).
Method: \(\sqrt{2}, A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}, 3\sqrt{2}\) are in A.P. (Note above). That is 5 terms with \(a_{1} = \sqrt{2}\) and \(a_{5} = 3\sqrt{2}\); find \(d\) from \(a_{5} = a_{1} + 4d\), then add \(d\) step by step.

Step 1: Find \(d\)
\[a_{5} = a_{1} + (5-1)d\]
\[3\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2} + 4d\]
\[4d = 2\sqrt{2}\]
\[d = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: \(3\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}\) (like terms, as \(3x - x = 2x\)); and \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Step 2: First mean
\[A_{1} = a_{1} + d = \sqrt{2} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{2 + 1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: write \(\sqrt{2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\) to get a common denominator.

Step 3: Second mean
\[A_{2} = A_{1} + d = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\]
Why: \(\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2 \times 2}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\) because \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\).

Step 4: Third mean
\[A_{3} = A_{2} + d = 2\sqrt{2} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{4 + 1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: \(2\sqrt{2} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\), then add the numerators.

Check:
One more step must give the last term: \(\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} = 3\sqrt{2}\). Correct.
The middle mean is the A.M. of the two ends: \(\frac{\sqrt{2} + 3\sqrt{2}}{2} = 2\sqrt{2} = A_{2}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(A\) is the A.M. between \(a\) and \(b\) when \(a, A, b\) are in A.P.; then \(A = \frac{a + b}{2}\).
2. \(n\) A.M.s between \(a\) and \(b\): \(a, A_{1}, \ldots, A_{n}, b\) form an A.P. of \(n + 2\) terms.
3. Find \(d\) from \(b = a + (n + 1)d\), then add \(d\) repeatedly.
4. Check: adding \(d\) to the last mean must give \(b\).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Using \(n\) instead of \(n + 2\) terms: for three means between \(a\) and \(b\), \(b\) is the 5th term, so \(b = a + 4d\), not \(a + 3d\).
2. Including \(a\) and \(b\) among the means: the means are only the numbers in between.
3. Surd slips: \(3\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}\), not \(3\).
